title: Refused service at Leo Poole's bar in San Francisco
summary: Cobb, his wife and Herbie Fields were refused service at a bar in the war years, and a suit they filed brought $100 that they gave to the NAACP.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: (Recording interruption)
Well, how -- how does one white guy travel good in a band where --
Oh, okay, that's all right, had no problems.
That was '48 or something?
It was the '40s.
Yeah, well, you talked about --
See, I stayed with Hamp until '47.
-- signifying and everything. You talked about signifying and so on. I mean what pals did he have?
You couldn't tell the difference in Herbie. I'll tell you why.
Oh, so he wasn't so bad then.
I'll tell you why. We went in Leo Poole's Bar in San Francisco, Herbie and a gal he had met. He'd fall in love with everybody he meets. And my wife -- that one right

there and myself and Leo and we never got served, and everybody come around because they thought all of us was Black. And they had a sign on there, "We reserve the right to refuse anyone service," during the war days.

So what we did, we laughed about it, but Madeline Green come in with a major in the Army. That was the singer in the group, and they went in the back to eat, and they were served before we got served, and here was a social worker in the place, and we went back to tell Madeline what happened at the bar. We never got served. We were between breaks on shows.

Everybody that come after us was served. So we told Madeline -- the social worker was there to witness it -- so we went to Gladys, and Gladys got the theater manager, and we filed a claim against Leo Poole's bar, and it cost me and Herbie $17.50 a piece, $35.00, and we said, we can't appear in court. The lawyer said, don't worry about. We got $100.00 for that situation. We turned it over to the NAACP.
(Laughter)
Right. Good.
That's the truth.
That's great.
But it was a joke, and he -- and we got a letter of apology from Leo Poole himself who wasn't there, but the guy that was his bartender was from Georgia. Now, you
put two and two together and take it from that.
